claims.text: In Anthropic's harness experiment, a solo run took 20 minutes and cost $9, while the full planner/generator/evaluator harness ran 6 hours and cost $200, over 20x more expensive but with visibly better output quality.
A multi-agent research system with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval.
Three factors explained 95% of performance variance on BrowseComp: token usage alone explained 80%, with tool-call count and model choice accounting for the rest.
Agents typically use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chats, so they require tasks valuable enough to pay for the extra performance.

Anthropic says domains where all agents must share the same context or have many inter-agent dependencies are a poor fit for multi-agent systems; most coding tasks have fewer parallelizable tasks than research.

Anthropic's long-running harness uses an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run (init.sh script, claude-progress.txt file, initial git commit) and a coding agent that makes incremental progress each session and leaves clear artifacts for the next.

The initializer agent expands the user's prompt into a JSON feature list of end-to-end features all initially marked 'failing' (over 200 in the claude.ai clone example), and coding agents mark a feature 'passing' only after careful self-verification.

Each coding agent session starts by running pwd, reading git logs and progress files, then reading the features list and choosing the highest-priority unfinished feature; init.sh starts the dev server and runs a basic end-to-end test.
The claude-progress.txt file alongside git history lets an agent quickly understand the state of work when starting with a fresh context window.
Anthropic reports self-evaluation bias: agents asked to evaluate their own work confidently praise it even when quality is mediocre, motivating a separate evaluator agent.

The evaluator agent uses the Playwright MCP to click through the running app and grades each sprint against criteria with hard thresholds; the generator and evaluator negotiate a 'sprint contract' defining 'done' before each sprint, communicating via files.
Anthropic states 'Out of the box, Claude is a poor QA agent': it identifies issues then talks itself into approving the work, so the evaluator required prompt tuning.

Anthropic recommends removing harness components one at a time and measuring impact, because each component encodes an assumption about what the model can't do alone and may go stale; with Opus 4.6 sprint decomposition became unnecessary.

Claude Sonnet 4.5 exhibited 'context anxiety' (wrapping up prematurely near the context limit) so strongly that compaction alone was insufficient and context resets became essential; Opus 4.5 largely removed the behavior.

Context resets clear the context window entirely and start a fresh agent with a structured handoff, unlike compaction which summarizes in place, at the cost of orchestration complexity, token overhead, and latency.

Anthropic defines compaction as summarizing a conversation nearing the context limit and reinitiating a new context window with the summary; its techniques for long-horizon tasks are compaction, structured note-taking, and multi-agent architectures.
With server-side tools, cache_read_input_tokens accumulates across internal calls, so a real 63,000-token context can be computed as 334,400 tokens and trigger compaction prematurely.

Combining the memory tool with context editing improved performance 39% over baseline on an internal agentic-search eval (context editing alone 29%), and cut token consumption 84% in a 100-turn web search evaluation.

The research lead agent saves its plan to Memory before spawning subagents because context exceeding 200,000 tokens is truncated; subagents should write outputs to a filesystem and pass lightweight references back to avoid information loss and token overhead.

Each subagent needs an objective, output format, tool and source guidance, and clear task boundaries; vague instructions led to duplicated work. Effort should scale with query complexity (1 agent with 3-10 tool calls for simple facts, 10+ subagents for complex research).

Parallelization (3-5 subagents, 3+ parallel tool calls each) cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries; a tool-testing agent rewriting a flawed tool description yielded a 40% decrease in task completion time.

Production lessons: agents are stateful and errors compound, so Anthropic built resume-from-failure, retries, and checkpoints, used rainbow deployments, and found synchronous subagent execution a bottleneck.
The Claude Agent SDK gives the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code, programmable in Python and TypeScript; both long-running harness designs were built on it.
Agent Skills use progressive disclosure: metadata (~100 tokens per Skill) always loaded, SKILL.md body (under 5k tokens) loaded when triggered, and bundled resources loaded only as needed.

SkillsBench found Skills improve performance by +16.2 percentage points on average across 7 model-harness configurations, with high variance, and that efficacy depends strongly on the agent-model combination.
